newsitem.title: USA: White House offers $18 billion more in Medicare cuts.
newsitem.headline: White House offers $18 billion more in Medicare cuts.

text.p: The White House and Congress reopened stalled budget negotiations Tuesday as the Clinton administration tried to nudge talks forward by offering an additional $18 billion in five-year Medicare cuts.
President Clinton is now willing to reduce Medicare by $100 billion over five years using more stringent congressional scoring, Republican aides said.
They said the new White House offer called for deeper cuts in Medicare payments to doctors, hospitals, skilled nursing facilities and other health providers.
"They (White House) also indicated a flexibility to do more and go beyond that," a House Republican aide said.
Medicare has been a main point of contention between Republicans and the White House.
Democrats attacked Republicans over Medicare during the 1996 campaign, charging their failed balanced budget plan would have decimated the popular health programme for seniors.

This time around, Republicans waited for the White House to move first. Clinton's original budget plan called for $100 billion in five-year Medicare cuts to providers. It was based on administration economic estimates.
Congressional analysts said the plan saved only $81.6 billion over that time frame. The administration Tuesday moved to the congressional figures.
The new White House offer calls for an additional $8.6 billion in cuts to hospitals, $1.2 billion to doctors, $2.9 billion to skilled nursing facilities and other changes, Republican aides said.
One source said White House and Republican aides also had a general discussion about proposals to require affluent seniors to pay higher Medicare premiums.

Earlier Tuesday, Clinton urged his negotiators to remain flexible on the numerous thorny issues from taxes to health-care spending as negotiating sessions got underway in a basement room of the Capitol.
Clinton's chief budget negotiator Frank Raines said the meeting "kicked off a good session" and reiterated the president's commitment to balance the budget by 2002.
The negotiators emerged after a 3-1/2 hour meeting agreeing to meet again but far from ready to shake hands on a deal to balance the budget in five years.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, called it "a solid meeting." Earlier he had said the decision to meet marked the beginning of a new phase in this year's budget negotiations.
The talks will resume Wednesday and are expected to go through the week, but Republicans warned they expected significant progress soon.
"Today was just a start. Clearly over the next few days we will see just how far the president and his negotiators will be willing to go," Domenici said.

House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, Republican of Ohio, said he has been preparing an alternative budget proposal and will seek out allies among conservative Democrats, if no compromise is reached with the White House.
"We are kind of at the end of the road. We are either going to see some progress made over the course of the week or we are not going to reach any agreement in the short term," Kasich said.

His Democratic counterpart on the House Budget Committee cautioned against reading too much into the meeting. "We are a long, long way off. We shouldn't raise false expectations today," Representative John Spratt, Democrat of South Carolina, said.
Before the budget session, Republican leaders emerged from a private meeting with statements that they remained committed to substantial tax cuts for families and investors.
